extracted.intended_audience: U.S. and foreign patent practitioners / patent attorneys who draft and litigate patent claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on recognizing when 35 U.S.C. §112(f) (means-plus-function) will be applied and how to draft claim language to avoid unintended invocation of §112(f), with practical examples and drafting tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory rule — 35 U.S.C. §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: An element in a claim may be expressed as a means or step for performing a specified function without recital of structure, material, or acts, and such a claim is construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim limitation is held to invoke §112(f), the claim is limited to the structure (and equivalents) actually disclosed in the specification; function-only claiming therefore risks narrowing claim scope to examples in the disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption from 'means for'/'step for' and the Williamson change
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, there was a strong presumption that using the words 'means for' or 'step for' invoked §112(f); Williamson (2015) weakened that strong presumption so that the determination is now more subjective and depends on whether a term is a 'nonce word' (a structureless generic term) used instead of 'means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Williamson the presumption still exists but is not dispositive — practitioners cannot rely solely on absence/presence of the literal words; must consider term meaning and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination standard — whether a POSITA would understand the term as a name for structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The key test is 'whether the words of the claim are understood by persons of ordinary skill in the art to have a sufficiently definite meaning as the name for structure' (Williamson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In litigation, expert declarations/testimony about what a POSITA would understand can be decisive in whether §112(f) applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of non-structural generic placeholders (MPEP examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP gives examples of non-structural generic placeholders that may invoke §112(f): 'mechanism for,' 'module for,' 'device for,' 'unit for,' 'component for,' 'element for,' 'member for,' 'apparatus for,' 'machine for,' or 'system for.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list is illustrative but not exhaustive; courts have applied these inconsistently case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coinage / nonce words; use inventor/industry terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Many §112(f) problems arise when practitioners coin generic terms instead of using the names that the inventor or the industry uses for components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the inventor what the industry calls the component and use that terminology in claims to reduce the risk that courts will treat the term as a non-structural placeholder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using 'for' as a transition between element name and functional language
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the word 'for' between an element name and functional language (e.g., 'system for doing X') can signal a functional limitation and invite §112(f) treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reword the limitation to remove 'for' or to include structural details immediately after the element name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid purely functional language; include structural detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Purely functional recitations (statements of what something does without structural context) increase the risk of means-plus-function interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim paragraph should do more than describe what something does — it should recite structure, connections, components, or location as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include structural language immediately after introducing a claim element
rubrics_metrics.description: After introducing an element, describe what the element looks like, what it is connected to, what its components are, and/or where it is located so the element reads as structural rather than purely functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: 'a fluid conduit extending between an inlet end that is connected to a water source and an outlet end that is connected to the water cannon' or 'a pipe, hose, or tube connected to the water cannon to define a water supply passage.' These phrasings avoid means-plus-function treatment while covering varied embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft multiple independent claims reciting different variations
rubrics_metrics.description: When uncertain whether a wording might invoke §112(f), draft multiple independent claims that recite different variations of the limitation (functional and structural variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This hedge increases the chance that at least some claims will be interpreted as structural and not limited to disclosed structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of structural terms that typically avoid §112(f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain terms connote structure and generally do not trigger §112(f); examples include 'clamp,' 'container,' 'lock,' 'conduit,' 'pipe,' 'hose,' and 'tube.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law supports that these terms are understood as structural by POSITA (e.g., TEK Global found 'conduit' recites sufficient structure). Prefer these over vague coined terms like 'system' where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences illustrated by practical example (water cannon / fluid delivery)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting 'a fluid delivery system for supplying water to the water cannon' may be treated as means-plus-function and limited to the corrugated hose disclosed in the specification (and equivalents), whereas reciting 'a fluid conduit' or explicitly 'pipe, hose, or tube' is less likely to invoke §112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete drafting alternatives that recite structure and connections; the example demonstrates how an apparently broad term can be narrowed by §112(f) unless structural language is included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts' inconsistent application and case law examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have differed in treatment of the same or similar terms across cases (e.g., some treat 'system' as a nonce word invoking §112(f), others may not). Relevant cases and authorities include Greenberg, Williamson, DYFAN v. Target, TEK Global, and cited MPEP guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because judicial outcomes vary, practitioners should (1) prefer structural wording, (2) document how a POSITA would understand terms (inventor statements, expert input), and (3) consider claim drafting redundancy to survive diverse interpretations.
